title: Matteo Ricci Writes On Friendship
text:
The Italian Jesuit Matteo Ricci reached China in 1582 and spent years in the south learning the language and the classics. He found that Chinese scholars valued learning and good conduct above everything, and that friendship between scholars was one of the five basic human relationships in Confucian thought. In 1595 he gave up the robes of a Buddhist monk he had first worn and dressed as a Confucian scholar instead.

That year, in the city of Nanchang, Ricci was invited to the court of a local prince of the imperial family, who asked him what people in the West thought about friendship. In answer Ricci wrote a little book in Chinese, the Jiaoyou lun, or Treatise on Friendship. It collected about a hundred short sayings on friendship drawn from Greek and Roman writers and Christian authors, rendered in polished Chinese. It opened with the idea that a friend is not another but half of oneself, a second self.

The book was copied and printed again and again, and won Ricci admiration among Chinese literati. It opened doors for him that preaching could not have opened. Ricci eventually reached Beijing, where he lived until his death in 1610.
lesson: To earn trust in another culture or group, start from what they already value and show that you share it. Common ground opens doors that argument cannot.
source: Matteo Ricci, Jiaoyou lun (Treatise on Friendship, 1595); Timothy Billings, trans., On Friendship: One Hundred Maxims for a Chinese Prince (2009)
